newsitem.title: UK: Russian gas oil heads to Asia, easing Europe glut.
newsitem.headline: Russian gas oil heads to Asia, easing Europe glut.

text.p: Up to 450,000 tonnes of Russian gas oil is being drawn eastwards by strong Indian and Asian demand, helping to ease the gas oil glut in Europe, traders said on Thursday.
Around 250,000 tonnes of the total is Baltic gas oil while 200,000 is from the Black Sea, they said.
The vast majority of Black Sea gas oil is destined for India, while the Baltic gas oil is headed for Singapore, one of the few areas in the world where refinery margins are currently strong.

The spread between Singapore gas oil and ARA gas oil has widened steadily since the beginning of February and is now over $32 a tonne. While freight rates are strong out of Northern Europe, tankers can be secured at a level that makes it a profitable route to trade.
A tanker was fixed earlier in the week to carry 75,000 tonnes of gas oil from Ventspils to Singapore at $1.8 million, or $24 a tonne, according to shipping sources.

Widespread refinery maintenance in Asia is also giving support to the draw, traders said. Around 950,000 barrels per day of Asian refining capacity will be in maintenance during March and April, according to a Reuter survey of refiners in the region.
A similar amount is expected to be shutdown in May.
The movement of Russian gas oil eastwards is already helping to support the European market.
"There has been a surplus of Russian gas oil, but arb moves have eaten it up," said a European trader.
"The eastern demand has neatly mopped up the Russian surplus," said another.
Premiums on Russian gas oil were largely unchanged on Thursday, but some dealers said there appeared to be less material on offer.
The outlook for Russian gas oil looks more encouraging on the back of the eastern draw. In addition refinery run cuts at several European refineries, due to bad margins, may also give support.
"We may see the odd refiner coming in looking to replace what he's lost from run cuts," said a gas oil broker.
Prices, which have fallen about $60 a tonne or 28 percent since the end of January, were not expected to rocket, but premiums could start to move away from screen discounts, traders thought.
